::: {.why}
Day 18 measured what backfilled membership costs; today the store stops doing it, which is the single largest correctness improvement available to the whole year.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Construct a universe as of any past date using only information available then, and defend the rule you used.
- Report the difference between your new point-in-time universe and today's membership backfilled, at three dates.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Implement the universe rule in qlib/store.py as `universe(as_of)`: if you have membership data, use it; if not, use a liquidity screen computed from trailing data only, such as the top N by 60-day median dollar volume among securities with a price history ending on or after that date. Either way the rule takes only past data as input.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Quantify the change: for 2010, 2015 and 2020, report the overlap between the point-in-time universe and today's membership backfilled, and the number of names in each that the other lacks. Then rerun your pairs screen on the point-in-time universe and note how the pair list changes.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
The store now returns a universe as of a date, built only from information available then. Every signal from here selects from that universe, so the survivorship problem is fixed in one place rather than remembered in twelve.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Your universe is today's S&P 500 taken back ten years. Quantify what that does to your results and say which direction it biases them.
:::
